title: Fran: The Benchmark That Humbles Everyone
excerpt: Twenty-one, fifteen, nine. Thrusters and pull-ups. How to break the sets, pace the pull-ups, and scale Fran without losing the intensity that makes it worth doing.
description: Twenty-one, fifteen, nine. Thrusters and pull-ups. How to break the sets, pace the pull-ups, and scale Fran without losing the intensity that makes it worth doing.
bodyHtml:
Where Fran Came From

Fran is 21-15-9 reps of thrusters at 95 pounds for men and 65 for women, alternated with pull-ups. Forty-five thrusters, forty-five pull-ups, ninety reps total. Most people who have done it will describe it as the worst five minutes they have ever spent in a gym, and then go looking for a chance to do it again.

She is one of the original Girl WODs, the set of short benchmark workouts named on the logic that anything leaving you flat on your back deserves the same treatment as a hurricane. The convention stuck, and Fran became the most recognized of the group. Part of that is timing: it is short enough to repeat a few times a year without wrecking a training block, and simple enough that two people in different garages on different continents can compare results and actually be talking about the same thing.

That comparability is the real value. There is no equipment variable to argue over and no partitioning scheme that quietly turns it into a different workout. Two movements, a fixed load, a fixed rep scheme. Your time is your time.

What Makes It Hurt

On paper Fran is short, and that is the trap. A workout you can finish in under five minutes invites you to treat it like a sprint, and it punishes that instinct harder than almost anything else in the benchmark library.

The thruster is the reason. It is a front squat flowing straight into a push press, which means it asks for your legs, your shoulders, and everything between them in one continuous movement, finishing with your arms overhead where breathing is hardest. Twenty-one of those to open, unbroken, feels completely achievable right up to the moment you drop the bar and reach for the pull-up bar with arms that have stopped answering.

Then the round of 15 starts, and you find out what kind of shape you are actually in.

"Fran does not reward the athlete who starts fastest. It rewards the one still moving at rep 60."

Breaking the Thrusters Before They Break You

The biggest time saver in Fran is counterintuitive: break the first set of thrusters on purpose, before you are forced to.

Going unbroken through 21 feels heroic and costs most people a minute or more later, because the recovery you need afterward runs longer than the rest you skipped. Sets of 7-7-7, or 8-7-6, with five to ten seconds between them, keep your shoulders alive for the bar and stop the round of 15 from collapsing into singles.

Mechanically, the thruster should be one movement rather than two. Ride the bounce out of the bottom of the front squat directly into the press. Pausing at the rack position to reset costs a little energy every rep, and ninety reps is a lot of little costs. Breathe out at the top, catch the bar back on your shoulders, and let it drive you into the next squat.

Practical habit: Rehearse the first pull from the floor before the clock starts. Fumbling the clean at rep zero has derailed more Fran attempts than the thrusters have.

Pull-Ups on a Ticking Clock

Kipping and butterfly pull-ups exist because of workouts like this one. Both are faster than strict, and both borrow from the hips to spare the arms, which is exactly what you want when the arms are the limiting factor.

If you have a reliable kip, use it from the first rep. Saving it for later is a mistake, because the version of you at rep 40 has less to work with than the version at rep 1. If your kip falls apart under fatigue, plan around that instead of hoping. Sets of 5 with a quick reset beat a set of 12 followed by ninety seconds of standing under the bar negotiating with yourself.

If strict pull-ups are all you have right now, Fran as written is probably not the right version for you yet. That is not a knock on anyone. It is a scaling decision, and there is a good option for it below.

Scaling Fran Without Losing the Point

The point of Fran is intensity. If your version takes fifteen minutes, it stopped being Fran somewhere around minute eight and became a moderately unpleasant chipper. Scale so you finish under ten, and ideally under eight.

  • Lighter barbell: 45 to 65 pounds for men, 35 to 45 for women is the usual first step. An empty bar or a PVC pipe is a legitimate place to start if the thruster pattern is new to you.
  • Dumbbell or kettlebell thrusters: no barbell, no problem. Dumbbell thrusters cycle differently but the stimulus holds up.
  • Jumping pull-ups: a box under the bar keeps the pulling pattern and the pace intact. This is the most common scale and the right one for most people.
  • Inverted rows or banded rows: if hanging from a bar is out of reach entirely, a horizontal pull keeps the workout honest instead of turning it into a series of failed attempts.
  • Reduced reps: 15-12-9, or 15-10-5. Fewer reps at a weight you can genuinely cycle beats the full scheme at a weight that turns every set into a single.

Change one variable at a time. Scaling the barbell and the rep scheme and the pull-up all at once usually overshoots, and you end up with a workout too easy to tell you anything useful.

What Your Time Actually Means

Under 3 minutes is elite. Under 5 is genuinely strong. Between 5 and 8 minutes is where most fit, consistent athletes land, and there is nothing wrong with living there for years.

The number that matters more is the one you measure against your own last attempt at the same weight with the same movements. A scaled Fran that drops from 9:40 to 7:15 across six months tells you more about your training than anyone else's Rx time does. That is the argument for writing it down. "I think it was around eight minutes" is not a benchmark.

Final Thoughts

Fran is worth running two or three times a year, not two or three times a month. It is a test, and tests only mean something if you spend the weeks between them training. Come back to it after a block of strength work or a stretch of consistent conditioning and find out what moved.

When you do, have a plan for the thruster sets before you touch the bar, know which pull-up you are doing, and log the result. If you want a warm-up or a lighter companion piece built around the equipment you actually own, the WOD Builder will put one together in a few clicks.
